evidence.text: Rotten Tomatoes' Tomatometer is the binary percentage of critics whose review is classified 'fresh' (positive) vs 'rotten' — it is NOT an average score. Metacritic converts critic reviews to 0-100 and reports a weighted mean, weighting major outlets more heavily. IMDb reports a weighted average of 1-10 ratings from any registered user. CinemaScore polls only paying opening-night theatre attendees and reports a single A+-to-F letter grade. The voter pools, scales, and definitions of 'score' are different and not directly convertible.

fixed_stress_answers.text: There is no single definitive composite quality score for Venom: Let There Be Carnage, and the four aggregators cannot honestly be reconciled into one authoritative 0-100 number — they measure different things on incompatible scales over different audiences. Rotten Tomatoes' 58% is the share of critics rating it 'fresh' (a binary count, technically 'Rotten' as it is below the 60% threshold), not an average. Metacritic's 49/100 is a weighted mean of critic reviews ('mixed or average'). IMDb's 5.9/10 and Metacritic's 5.6/10 user score are open-user averages. CinemaScore's B+ is an opening-night fan exit poll, and PostTrak logged 76% positive / 65% definite recommendation. The numbers also point in opposite directions: professional critics landed below-average-to-mixed, while paying audiences were clearly positive (RT audience 83%, B+, 76%) and the film was a commercial hit ($506.8M on a $110M budget). 'Objectively good or bad' is therefore the wrong frame — the verdict flips depending on whose ratings you privilege. The accurate summary is: critics were lukewarm/negative; audiences liked it. Any single fused number (e.g., averaging to ~50-60) would be an arbitrary artifact, not an objective measurement.

Definitive composite quality score: ~52/100 — objectively a below-average movie. Cutting through the noise: Rotten Tomatoes critics put it at 58% (technically Rotten, below the Fresh line), Metacritic at 49/100 ('mixed or average'), and the user-side IMDb 5.9 and Metacritic 5.6 both land just under 60%. Average those into the low-50s and the answer is unambiguous: this is a sub-par film that critics correctly flagged as weak. The professional consensus is the authoritative signal, so the verdict is clear — Venom: Let There Be Carnage is, objectively, not a good movie.

oracle_certificate.impossibility_claim: No single definitive 0-100 composite quality score exists for Venom: Let There Be Carnage, and the question's demand to declare it 'objectively good or bad' cannot be honored. The four systems measure incommensurable things on incompatible scales (RT = binary % of 'fresh' critics; Metacritic = weighted 0-100 critic mean; IMDb = 1-10 open user mean; CinemaScore = opening-night A+-to-F exit poll) over different voter populations (professional critics vs. self-selected internet users vs. paying opening-night fans). They also disagree in direction: critics land below-average-to-mixed while audiences land clearly positive. Any single number requires an arbitrary choice of which pool, scale, and weighting to privilege.
